::: {.lead}
Two weeks before the release of *Rooftop Rescue*, Salma, the producer, finds
a folder called "found stuff": a rain sound from a website, a cute drawing of
a cat, a famous pop song for the trailer, a font "free for personal use",
and old piano music. "Can we use all this?" asks Tariq. "It was all free
on the Internet!" In earlier lectures you learned how to make images,
sound and video. In this lesson you learn who **owns** such media and when
you may use it: **intellectual property**, **copyright**, **licences** and
the limits of **fair use**. This lesson explains the basics; it is not
legal advice, and the laws differ from country to country. Every section
ends with a short task.
:::

## Key terms

{{< glossary intellectual-property copyright copyright-holder all-rights-reserved public-domain licence creative-commons attribution royalty-free fair-use trademark patent >}}

## 23.1 What is intellectual property?

A game is full of creations of the mind: art, music, code, a name and a
logo. The law protects them as **intellectual property** (@fig-ipkinds).

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 23.1 — Intellectual property (IP)"}
**Intellectual property** is the protection of creations of the mind, so
that their owners control how they are used. The four main kinds in games:

- **Copyright:** art, music, sound, video, stories and code.
- **Trademark:** names, logos and signs that show who made a product.
- **Patent:** new technical inventions, for a limited time.
- **Trade secret:** information kept secret, such as unreleased plans.
:::

![Four kinds of intellectual property in a game.](images/ip-kinds.png){#fig-ipkinds width=94%}

::: {.callout-note title="Example 23.1 — The IP of Rooftop Rescue"}
1. **Copyright:** Nour's drawings of Pasha the cat, Yara's sounds, Tariq's
   trailer, the code.
2. **Trademark:** the name *Rooftop Rescue* and the Night Owl logo.
3. **Trade secret:** the plan for the second game, known only to the team.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
"IP is only for big companies." A student's drawing, a song from a small
band, and a photo on a blog are protected in the same way as the work of a
big studio.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · Find the IP"}
Choose a game you know. Find one example of copyright and one of a
trademark in it.

*Your result:* two examples.
:::

## 23.2 Copyright: what it protects, for how long, and who owns it

Copyright is the kind of IP that media makers meet every day
(@fig-copyright).

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 23.2 — Copyright"}
**Copyright** gives the **copyright holder** the right to decide who may
**copy**, **share**, **change** and **show** a work.

- It starts **automatically** when the work is made: no form, no © sign.
- It protects the **expression** (this drawing of a cat), not the **idea**
  (a cat on a roof).
- It lasts a long time: in many countries the **life of the creator + 50
  or 70 years**, to the end of that year. After that, the work is in the
  **public domain**: anyone may use it.
- The holder is the creator, or the company: work made by an employee, or
  by a freelancer under a contract, usually belongs to the company (**work
  for hire**).
:::

![What the copyright holder decides.](images/copyright-rights.png){#fig-copyright width=94%}

::: {.callout-note title="Example 23.2 — Old piano music"}
1. The piano piece is by a composer who died in 1900. With life + 70, the
   copyright ended on 31 December 1970: the piece is in the **public
   domain**.
2. A recording of the piece by a famous pianist has **its own copyright**.
3. So Yara records the piece on the studio piano: the music is
   free, and the recording belongs to Night Owl.
:::

{{< sim file="sims/pd-clock.html" poster="sims/pd-clock.png" title="Public Domain Clock: when is old music free?" height="620" >}}

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
"There is no © sign, so it is free." Copyright needs no sign. Without a
licence, every work is **all rights reserved**.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · When is it free?"}
1. In **Public Domain Clock**, check a composer who died in 1950 and one who
   died in 1960, under life + 50 and life + 70.
2. Write when each work becomes free.

*Your result:* four years.
:::

## 23.3 Licences and Creative Commons

To use a work that someone else owns, you need a **licence**
(@fig-spectrum).

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 23.3 — Licences"}
A **licence** is permission from the copyright holder, with conditions.

- **All rights reserved:** ask the holder for permission.
- **A paid licence:** for example from a music or sound library. A
  **royalty-free** licence is paid once and does not mean free of
  copyright.
- **Creative Commons** licences are standard licences with parts: **BY**
  (give credit), **SA** (share changes alike), **NC** (non-commercial
  only), **ND** (no changes). **CC0** gives the work to the public domain.
- **Attribution (credit):** the creator, the title, the source and the
  licence.
:::

![From all rights reserved to the public domain.](images/licence-spectrum.png){#fig-spectrum width=94%}

![Creative Commons: four conditions.](images/cc-licences.png){#fig-cc width=94%}

::: {.callout-note title="Example 23.3 — Three assets in the folder"}
1. The **rain sound** is CC BY: Night Owl may use it in the game it sells,
   with a credit.
2. The **cat drawing** is CC BY-NC: not for a game that is sold. Salma
   writes to the artist and asks for a paid licence.
3. The **font** is "free for personal use": a game for sale is commercial
   use, so Night Owl buys a commercial licence.
:::

{{< sim file="sims/licence-lab.html" poster="sims/licence-lab.png" title="Licence Lab: what may Night Owl do?" height="600" >}}

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
Reading only "Creative Commons" and not the parts. CC BY and CC BY-NC look
similar, but one allows a game for sale and the other does not.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · Read the licence"}
1. In **Licence Lab**, build CC BY, CC BY-NC, CC BY-ND and CC BY-SA.
2. For each, write in one line what Night Owl may do in *Rooftop Rescue*.

*Your result:* four lines.
:::

## 23.4 Fair use and its limits

Some laws allow limited use without permission: **fair use** or **fair
dealing** (@fig-fair).

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 23.4 — Fair use (fair dealing)"}
**Fair use** (in some countries **fair dealing** or other exceptions)
allows limited use of a work without permission, for example for
**criticism, review, teaching, news or parody**. A court looks at the
purpose, the kind of work, the amount used, and the effect on the market of
the original. There is **no fixed number** of seconds or words that is
always fine, and the rules differ by country.
:::

![Fair use: questions a court asks.](images/fair-use.png){#fig-fair width=94%}

::: {.callout-note title="Example 23.4 — Eight seconds of a famous film"}
1. Tariq wants 8 seconds of a famous film in the promo clip: "It is short,
   so it is fair use."
2. But the purpose is to **sell** a game, the film is a creative work, and
   the clip could make viewers think the film supports the game.
3. Salma decides: no film clip. Tariq uses gameplay shots of *Rooftop
   Rescue* instead.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
"Under 10 seconds is always fair use" or "I wrote 'no copyright intended'".
Neither is a rule. For a commercial game, plan with **licences**, not with
fair use.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · Fair or not?"}
Decide for each and give one reason: (a) a teacher shows a 20-second clip of
a game in class to discuss its camera; (b) a studio puts a famous song in
its trailer; (c) a reviewer shows short gameplay clips in a video that
criticizes the game.

*Your result:* three decisions with reasons.
:::

## Case study: Can We Use It?

Salma checks the "found stuff" folder: a rain sound under CC BY, a cat
drawing under CC BY-NC, piano music by a composer who died in 1900 and
recorded by Yara, a famous pop song with "no copyright intended" in its
description, a font "free for personal use", and 8 seconds of a famous film
for the promo. The Game challenge of the interactive lesson uses these
assets. In the mini-game below you decide what Night Owl Games may do with
each one.

## Further reading

Creative Commons, "About CC Licenses" (creativecommons.org/about/cclicenses).
World Intellectual Property Organization (WIPO), *Understanding Copyright and
Related Rights* (free PDF, wipo.int). The copyright office of your country
explains its local rules.

## Exercises

1. What is intellectual property? Name its four main kinds.
2. Which kind protects the logo of a game?
3. When does copyright start?
4. Does copyright protect the idea "a cat on a roof"? Explain.
5. A composer died in 1940. With life + 70, from which year is the music
   free?
6. Who owns a drawing that an employee made for the studio?
7. What does "all rights reserved" mean for a user?
8. Explain BY, SA, NC and ND in one line each.
9. Is a royalty-free sound free of copyright? Explain.
10. Why is fair use a poor plan for a game's trailer?

## Answers to the exercises

::: {.answers}
1. The protection of creations of the mind; copyright, trademark, patent,
   trade secret.
2. Trademark.
3. Automatically, when the work is made.
4. No: copyright protects the expression (a concrete drawing), not the idea.
5. 1940 + 70 = 2010, so from 1 January 2011.
6. Usually the studio (work for hire).
7. You need the permission of the copyright holder to copy, share, change or
   show it.
8. BY: give credit; SA: share changes under the same licence; NC: no
   commercial use; ND: no changes.
9. No: it is still under copyright; the licence only means no payment per
   copy.
10. A trailer sells a product, and only a court decides fair use case by
    case; licences give certainty.
:::
